## Step A (reference) — Switch KDF to Argon2id (~2 min)

**Why:** Argon2id is OWASP's top recommendation for password hashing. It resists GPU/ASIC-based cracking far better than the default PBKDF2. Do this BEFORE loading Tier-1 credentials so they all get the stronger crypto from the start.

1. Go to **vault.bitwarden.com** and sign in.
2. Click **Settings** (left sidebar) → **Security** → **Keys** tab.
3. Under **Key Derivation Function**, change **PBKDF2** → **Argon2id**.
4. Leave the defaults: m=64 MiB, t=3, p=4 (Bitwarden's recommended values).
5. Click **Change KDF**.
6. Enter your master password to confirm.
7. Wait a few seconds — it re-encrypts your entire vault.
8. **Verify:** The page shows "Argon2id" as the active KDF. Your vault still opens normally.

✅ **Done when:** KDF shows Argon2id, vault unlocks normally, no errors.

## Step B (reference) — Create free 2-person org + invite Sarah (CORRECTED) (~5 min)

**Why:** A free 2-person organization lets Sarah access shared household credentials in up to 2 collections at NO cost. This may eliminate the need for the $40/yr Family plan (H4 decision). Sarah gets her own free account; you put shared items in org collections. **The org is the Azzopardi Reynolds household org — NOT a Seddon org. There is no Seddon collection, because you hold no Seddon logins.**

1. Go to **vault.bitwarden.com** → **Settings** → **Organizations**.
2. Click **New Organization**.
3. Name it for the household, e.g. **"Azzopardi Reynolds"** (the household org).
4. Under **Plan**, choose **Free** (2 users, 2 collections — free forever).
5. Create **Collection 1:** "Household Shared" (utility logins, shared household accounts).
6. Create **Collection 2 (optional):** a second household-scope collection if you have another shared category (e.g. "Azzopardi-Reynolds Finance"). Keep collections household-scope. **Do NOT create a "Legal Case Shared" collection — that was a wrong assumption; you hold no Seddon legal credentials.**
7. Click **Invite User** → enter Sarah's email → role: **User**.
8. Assign her to the household collection(s).
9. Sarah receives an email → she creates her own free Bitwarden account → accepts the invite.
10. **Move shared items:** In your vault, select an item → **Move to Organization** → choose the household collection.

✅ **Done when:** Org exists (named for the household), Sarah invited, household collection(s) created, at least one shared item moved.

**Note:** Items in the free org do NOT get TOTP code generation or vault health reports. Those are Premium features. If you need them on shared items, that's when you'd upgrade to Family ($40/yr). For now, free is fine.

## Step C — (OPTIONAL) Premium upgrade + Emergency Access (~$10/yr, ~5 min)

**Why:** Emergency Access lets Sarah request access to your vault if something happens to you, after a wait period you set. This matters for household continuity. This is a SEPARATE decision from H4 (Sarah's own login) — it's about what happens to your vault if you can't respond. (The earlier note tying this to the "legal/financial sensitivity of the Seddon source" is removed — emergency access is for the household vault, not the Seddon documents, which live separately.)

1. Go to **vault.bitwarden.com** → **Settings** → **Premium Membership**.
2. Click **Upgrade to Premium** → $10/year → enter payment.
3. Go to **Settings** → **Emergency Access**.
4. Click **Add Trusted Contact** → enter Sarah's email.
5. Choose access type: **View** (recommended) or **Takeover**.
6. Set wait period: **7 days** (balances "on vacation without signal" vs. genuine emergency).
7. Sarah receives an email → she accepts.
8. **Test it once a year:** Sarah requests access → you deny it (to confirm the flow works).

✅ **Done when:** Premium active, Sarah added as trusted contact, wait period set to 7 days.

**If you skip this:** Your vault is still fully functional on free tier. Emergency Access is the only feature you lose. You can upgrade later anytime.

## Step D — First encrypted export backup (~3 min)

**Why:** A Password-protected encrypted JSON export is your disaster-recovery backup. It supports the "quarantine irreversibility" requirement — if Bitwarden ever disappears, you can import this into any other password manager. Do this after Steps A–C so the backup reflects your hardened setup.

**Where to store it:** D: drive (FullyDecrypted, cannot be BitLockered per your environment) or an external encrypted drive. NEVER in `ai-context/` or `agent-workdir/` where the AI system can read it.

1. Open the **Bitwarden desktop app** (or web vault → Tools → Export).
2. Go to **Tools** → **Export Vault**.
3. Choose format: **.json (Encrypted)**.
4. Choose encryption type: **Password protected** (NOT "Account restricted" — that only re-imports to the same account; "Password protected" is portable).
5. Enter a backup password — make it STRONGER than your master password (you rarely need to type it, so length is not a daily burden).
6. Click **Export** → save to `D:\backups\bitwarden-vault-2026-08-15.json`.
7. **Store the backup password SEPARATELY** from the backup file:
   - Physical safe, or
   - Split across two locations, or
   - With a trusted person (NOT in the same vault it backs up).
8. **Verify:** Try importing the file into a test Bitwarden account (or just confirm it opens with the backup password). Then delete the test import.

✅ **Done when:** Encrypted JSON file exists on D: drive, backup password stored separately, file opens with the backup password.
